subject: Computer Networking
title: WebSockets for Real-Time
description: A fast breakdown of WebSockets for Real-Time for builders.

hook.text: HTTP is request-response. But chat apps need the server to push messages instantly. WebSockets do that.

buildup.text: A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request, then upgrades to a persistent two-way connection.

discovery.text: Once open, both sides send messages freely. No request needed. Data flows in real time, low latency.

twist.text: WebSockets stay open for hours. HTTP connections close after each response. Different lifetime, different use.

climax.text: Stock tickers, multiplayer games, and collaborative editors all rely on WebSocket connections.

punchline.text: WebSockets keep the line open. Real-time web, no polling.

quiz.question: How does a WebSocket connection begin?
options: As an HTTP request that upgrades to a persistent connection
As a direct TCP socket bypassing HTTP entirely
As a UDP packet sent to the server

details.summary: WebSockets establish a persistent, full-duplex connection between browser and server after an HTTP upgrade handshake. Both sides can send messages at any time without the overhead of new HTTP requests. This enables real-time features like chat, live dashboards, and multiplayer games.
details.whyItMatters: WebSockets transformed the web from request-response only into a platform for real-time applications. They power the live, interactive experiences that modern users expect.
takeaways: Full-duplex communication lets both sides send messages freely
An HTTP upgrade handshake transitions to the WebSocket protocol
Persistent connections eliminate per-message HTTP overhead

faq.question: When should you use WebSockets vs polling?
faq.answer: Use WebSockets when data flows frequently in both directions: chat, gaming, collaborative editing. Use long polling or Server-Sent Events for lower-frequency one-directional updates: notifications, live feeds.

faq.question: How do WebSockets scale?
faq.answer: Each WebSocket holds a persistent TCP connection, consuming server memory. Scaling to millions of connections requires efficient event-driven servers, connection pooling, and pub/sub systems like Redis to distribute messages across server instances.
